inputs.question: Item table size and GET /items request rate?

known: create_engine is called with no pool arguments (backend/app/core/db.py:7).
Item.owner_id has a foreign key but no index in the model or any migration.
List endpoints accept an unbounded limit query parameter.
unknown: Argon2 parameters in the deployed pwdlib version
assumed: Item table grows beyond a size where a sequential scan matters (affects PERF-001).
Login and password-change traffic is concurrent enough to overlap hashing (affects PERF-003).
derived: Maximum connections the service can open = 4 workers x (default pool 5 + overflow 10) = 60, assuming SQLAlchemy defaults; from the Dockerfile worker count and unmodified create_engine.

decision_changing_questions.question: Expected row count of the item table and the share of requests hitting GET /items?
decision_changing_questions.what_it_would_change: Raises or lowers PERF-001 and PERF-002 severity.

decision_changing_questions.question: Peak concurrent logins and password changes per second?
Is outbound SMTP reliable and is password recovery exposed publicly?

root_causes.description: Item listing and owner-scoped deletes filter on an unindexed foreign key.
List endpoints have no upper bound on page size and use offset pagination.
Slow synchronous work (password hashing, SMTP) runs inside request handlers while a DB session and pooled connection are held, on a default-sized pool.

findings.problem: item.owner_id is a foreign key with no index, yet every non-superuser GET /items runs a COUNT and an ordered, filtered page query on it, and user deletion deletes items by owner_id.
findings.performance_principle: Selective lookups on a growing collection need an access path proportional to the result, not to the table.

evidence.statement: owner_id declared with foreign_key and ondelete only, no index=True.
The only index created in migrations is ix_user_email; none on item.owner_id.
Count and page query both filter on Item.owner_id and order by created_at desc.
delete_user runs DELETE FROM item WHERE owner_id = :id; ON DELETE CASCADE also needs the lookup.
No runtime evidence (no EXPLAIN, no row counts) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Item table large enough that a full scan is costly (assumed, size unknown), and clients list items frequently. Superuser listing has no filter and is unaffected by the index.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched models, migrations and compose for any index or planner hint on item.owner_id; none found.
Row count unknown; on small tables the planner prefers a sequential scan anyway.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If the item table stays in the low thousands of rows, a sequential scan is cheap and the index adds only write overhead.
findings.recommendation: Add an Alembic migration creating an index on item(owner_id), ideally composite (owner_id, created_at DESC) to serve the filtered ordered page and the count; declare it in the model so it is not lost.

alternatives.why: Serves filter, sort and cascade deletes in one structure.
Simpler, removes the scan but leaves a sort step.
Masks the missing access path and adds invalidation.

findings.trade_offs: Extra write cost and storage on item inserts/updates; on a large live table create the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

validation.metric: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) plan node type and execution time for the owner-scoped item page query
validation.expectation: Seq Scan on item replaced by an index scan; rows read proportional to the page size.
validation.falsifier: Plan already uses an index (added outside the migrations) or the table is small enough that timing is unchanged.
validation.guard: Query-plan or p95 latency check on GET /api/v1/items in staging with seeded data.

commands.command: SELECT relname, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'item';
commands.purpose: Learn the item table size to decide severity.

commands.command: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM item WHERE owner_id = '<an owner uuid>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100;
commands.purpose: Confirm the current plan (ANALYZE executes the query; use a replica or staging).

findings.problem: skip and limit on GET /items and GET /users are unvalidated integers with no maximum, so one request can read and serialize the whole table; offset pagination also rescans skipped rows, and a COUNT runs on every page.
findings.performance_principle: Work per request must be bounded by a server-enforced limit, not a client-chosen one.

evidence.statement: limit: int = 100 has no upper bound (no Query(le=...)); offset(skip).limit(limit) is applied directly.
Same pattern for users listing, plus a full COUNT per call.
Each row is validated twice in Python: ItemPublic.model_validate in the handler and again via response_model.

findings.conditions: Any authenticated client (superuser for GET /users) can request a large limit; matters when the table holds more rows than fit comfortably in a worker's memory and time budget. Table size unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for global pagination caps and middleware; none in repo. A reverse proxy config outside the repo could not be checked.
Non-superuser item listing is bounded by the user's own item count, which limits blast radius.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Only authenticated users reach it, and the bundled frontend uses the default of 100; abuse requires a deliberate client.
findings.recommendation: Constrain limit with Query(ge=1, le=<server maximum>) and skip with ge=0; consider keyset pagination on (created_at, id) if deep pages are needed.

alternatives.why: Removes the unbounded work with a one-line change.
Fixes deep offset cost but changes the API contract.

findings.trade_offs: Clients requesting more than the cap must page; keyset pagination breaks arbitrary page jumps.

validation.metric: Response time and worker memory for GET /api/v1/items?limit=<large> against a seeded table
validation.expectation: Requests above the cap are rejected with 422 and cost is bounded.
validation.falsifier: A proxy or other layer already caps limit, or large limits run in the same time as the default.
validation.guard: Test asserting limit above the cap returns 422.

findings.problem: Argon2 password hashing and verification, a CPU- and memory-heavy operation, runs in sync handlers while the request's DB session already holds a checked-out pooled connection, on an engine left at default pool settings.
findings.performance_principle: Do not hold a scarce shared resource (pooled connection) across slow work that does not need it.

evidence.statement: authenticate queries the user (opening a transaction on a pooled connection) and then calls verify_password; the session is released only at request end.
The dummy hash used for unknown users encodes m=65536,t=3,p=4, i.e. a 64 MiB, 3-pass Argon2 verification per attempt.
update_password_me verifies and hashes with current_user (and thus a connection) loaded; create_user and signup hash inside the request too.
Engine created with no pool_size/max_overflow/pool_timeout arguments.

Derivation: 4 workers (Dockerfile CMD) x default pool 5 + overflow 10 = 60 connections maximum if SQLAlchemy defaults apply; sync handlers run in a threadpool that can hold more concurrent requests than the pool allows.

findings.conditions: Concurrent logins, password changes or sign-ups from many clients (credential stuffing or a login burst); hashing time per request is unmeasured and depends on cores.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for rate limiting or login throttling; none found.
Hash cost is deliberate for security; the issue is when it runs relative to the connection. Actual pool wait was not measured.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Login is a small share of traffic for most deployments, and 60 connections may exceed the concurrent logins ever seen.
findings.recommendation: In authenticate, read the user and release the transaction (commit or close) before verify_password; add login rate limiting; size pool_size/max_overflow/pool_timeout explicitly against Postgres max_connections.

alternatives.option: Release the connection before hashing and set explicit pool sizes
alternatives.why: Directly removes the long hold on the shared pool.

alternatives.option: Run hashing in a dedicated process pool
alternatives.why: Adds operational complexity before need is measured.

findings.trade_offs: Extra session handling and a second connection acquisition for the rehash write path; rate limiting adds shared state.

validation.metric: Pool checked-out count and p95 of POST /login/access-token under a concurrent login load test
validation.expectation: Fewer connection-seconds held per login; less pool wait under concurrent logins.
validation.falsifier: Pool wait is negligible at target login concurrency, or hashing takes negligible time.

commands.command: cd backend && uv run python -c "import time; from app.core.security import get_password_hash; t=time.perf_counter(); get_password_hash('example-password'); print(time.perf_counter()-t)"
commands.purpose: Measure the actual hash cost on target hardware.

findings.problem: Password recovery (unauthenticated) and user creation send SMTP mail synchronously inside the request, with a DB session open and no explicit SMTP timeout configured.
findings.performance_principle: Do not make user-facing requests wait on a slow, unreliable external dependency, and always bound waits.

evidence.statement: recover_password looks up the user, then calls send_email inline before responding.
smtp_options sets host, port, tls and credentials only; no timeout.
No runtime evidence of SMTP latency exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: SMTP provider slow or unreachable, and recovery requests for registered addresses arrive at a rate that occupies the worker threadpool (assumed).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for background task or queue usage around send_email; none. The default timeout of the emails library was not verified from the repo.
Emails are only sent when SMTP_HOST is configured (emails_enabled).

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Recovery requests are rare in most apps, and a healthy SMTP relay returns quickly.
findings.recommendation: Set an explicit SMTP timeout and move sending to FastAPI BackgroundTasks (or a queue if delivery guarantees are needed) so the response and DB connection are not tied to SMTP latency.

alternatives.why: Minimal change; takes SMTP off the critical path.
Better delivery guarantees but heavy for this template.

findings.trade_offs: Send failures are no longer surfaced to the caller; failed sends need logging.

validation.metric: Latency of POST /password-recovery/{email} with a delayed SMTP stub
validation.expectation: Response time independent of SMTP delay after the change.
validation.falsifier: Response already independent of SMTP delay (library timeout is short and mail is fast).
validation.guard: Test with a slow SMTP stub asserting response under a bound.
